extracted.intended_audience: general readers (consumers, journalists, activists, policymakers) interested in environmental marketing and corporate sustainability claims
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance on what constitutes greenwashing, how it presents (characteristics, types, and common indicators), examples across industries, and regulatory / deterrence responses for evaluating or producing environmental claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of greenwashing
rubrics_metrics.description: Greenwashing (also called green sheen) is a form of advertising or marketing spin that deceptively uses green PR and green marketing to persuade the public that an organization's products, goals, or policies are environmentally friendly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used as the baseline criterion: an environmental claim or presentation is greenwashing when it is deceptive — i.e., presents an organisation or product as more environmentally friendly than it actually is. Examples include selective disclosure, misleading advertising, and exaggerated claims (e.g., Volkswagen 'clean diesel' emissions scandal).

rubrics_metrics.name: Occurrence criterion — advertising outweighs actual practices
rubrics_metrics.description: Greenwashing occurs when an organization spends significantly more resources on 'green' advertising than on environmentally sound practices.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate the balance between outward communications and concrete operational/environmental improvements. A red flag is heavy investment in green messaging with little evidence of substantive environmental action.

rubrics_metrics.name: UN indicators — claiming future milestones without plans
rubrics_metrics.description: Claiming that the company will achieve future environmental milestones while not putting sufficient plans in place to do so.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether commitments are backed by timebound, verifiable plans and interim milestones. Unsupported future promises (e.g., vague net-zero targets without credible pathways) count as potential greenwashing.

rubrics_metrics.name: UN indicators — intentional vagueness / vague claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Being intentionally vague about operations or using vague claims that cannot be specifically proven (like saying they are 'environmentally friendly' or 'green').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look for precise language, quantitative metrics, and definitional clarity. Vague adjectives without qualifiers or evidence (e.g., 'eco-friendly', 'natural') are suspect and should trigger requests for substantiation.

rubrics_metrics.name: UN indicators — claiming absence of harms that are irrelevant
rubrics_metrics.description: Saying that a product does not contain harmful materials or use harmful practices that they would not use anyway.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Check whether the claimed absence is meaningful (material and relevant to overall environmental performance) rather than trivial or already industry-standard.

rubrics_metrics.name: UN indicators — highlighting a single good attribute while ignoring others
rubrics_metrics.description: Highlighting one thing the company does well regarding the environment while not doing anything else.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess the product or firm's full environmental footprint rather than isolated attributes. Single-attribute claims (e.g., 'made with recycled plastic' while other impacts are large) may be misleading (hidden trade-off).

rubrics_metrics.name: UN indicators — presenting regulatory-minimum performance as exceptional
rubrics_metrics.description: Promoting products that meet regulatory minimums as if peer products do not.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Verify whether the claimed advantage is genuinely better than standard/legal requirements. Marketing that treats compliance as superiority may be misleading.

rubrics_metrics.name: TerraChoice 'Hidden Trade-off' (sin)
rubrics_metrics.description: "Hidden Trade-off" — claims a product is 'green' based on an unreasonably narrow set of attributes without attention to other critical environmental issues.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate trade-offs across life-cycle stages and impact categories. A single favorable attribute does not make a product overall sustainable; watch for omission of major impacts.

rubrics_metrics.name: TerraChoice 'No Proof' (sin)
rubrics_metrics.description: "No proof" — a claim that cannot be substantiated by easily accessible information or a reliable third-party certification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Require accessible evidence or credible third-party verification for environmental claims. Lack of substantiation is a core indicator of greenwashing.

rubrics_metrics.name: TerraChoice 'Vagueness' (sin)
rubrics_metrics.description: "Vagueness" — a poorly defined or broad claim that the consumer will likely misunderstand, such as 'all-natural.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer specific, defined claims (e.g., percentage recycled content, standard names). Vague terms without definition should be treated as suspect.

rubrics_metrics.name: TerraChoice 'Worshipping False Labels' (sin)
rubrics_metrics.description: "Worshipping False Labels" — a claim that, through words or images, gives the impression of a third‑party endorsement where none exists.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Check whether labels/endorsements are real, from independent organisations, and not self-created or misleadingly presented. Look for accreditation details and links to certifying bodies.

rubrics_metrics.name: TerraChoice 'Irrelevance' (sin)
rubrics_metrics.description: "Irrelevance" — a claim that may be truthful but unimportant or unhelpful to consumers seeking environmentally preferable products.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Determine whether the claimed attribute materially affects environmental performance. Irrelevant facts (e.g., 'CFC‑free' for products never using CFCs) can mislead consumers.

rubrics_metrics.name: TerraChoice 'Lesser of Two Evils' (sin)
rubrics_metrics.description: "Lesser of Two Evils" — a claim that may be true within the product category, but risks distracting consumers from the more significant environmental impact of the category.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider category-level impacts; a marginally 'greener' tobacco product or gasoline-powered vehicle may still be harmful. Evaluate relative claims in context.

rubrics_metrics.name: TerraChoice 'Fibbing' (sin)
rubrics_metrics.description: "Fibbing" — a claim that is simply false.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Fact-check categorical claims. Falsely stated attributes (e.g., fabricated certifications) are straightforward greenwashing and may carry legal risk.

rubrics_metrics.name: Type — Direct greenwashing
rubrics_metrics.description: Direct greenwashing occurs when a firm's own processes are inconsistent with its environmental claims and lead to blaming the entire company and low intention to invest.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compare public claims with corporate operations, policies, and independent audit results. Direct mismatch between rhetoric and operations is a major indicator.

rubrics_metrics.name: Type — Indirect greenwashing
rubrics_metrics.description: Indirect greenwashing happens when a supplier makes false environmental claims, thus the company it supplies is negatively impacted even though the company itself did not commit the misconduct.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess supply chain claims and supplier verification. A firm's sustainability reputation can be harmed by supplier misstatements; due diligence of suppliers is necessary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Type — Vicarious greenwashing
rubrics_metrics.description: Vicarious greenwashing occurs when a 'green' company partners with a non-environmentally friendly supplier; the company is held liable for the supplier's misconduct because of its stated commitment to sustainability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examine partnerships and contractual sustainability obligations; PR alliances with poorly performing partners can constitute misleading association.

rubrics_metrics.name: Type — Product-level greenwashing (claim and executional)
rubrics_metrics.description: Product-level greenwashing focuses on products/services. 'Claim greenwashing' uses misleading statements about environmental benefits; 'executional greenwashing' relies on visuals and symbols (green colours, nature imagery) to mislead consumers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For claims, verify technical substantiation and certifications. For executional cues, don't rely on imagery—seek hard evidence. Watch industries (fashion, cosmetics) where symbolic cues are commonly used.

rubrics_metrics.name: Type — Firm-level greenwashing
rubrics_metrics.description: Firm-level greenwashing happens at the organizational level when a firm uses advertising and campaigns to promote sustainability while still having operations that damage the environment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate corporate-wide emissions, operations, lobbying, and business model alignment with claimed sustainability. Assess reputation-risk when campaigns obscure harmful core activities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Symbolic / imagery-based greenwashing
rubrics_metrics.description: Symbolic greenwashing ('imagery substitutes evidence')—the use of nature imagery, green colour palettes, and aesthetic association to create the impression of environmental benefit where factual support is lacking.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat evocative visuals and nature motifs as insufficient evidence; require linked facts, data, or certification. Social media posts and influencer content that rely on aesthetic signals should be probed for substantiation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of unregulated or undefined terminology
rubrics_metrics.description: The continued use of unregulated terminology such as 'clean', 'natural', and 'eco-friendly' which lack scientific definitions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Demand definitions and evidence when such terms are used. Regulators and guidance documents often require clarity; unqualified terms are common red flags.

rubrics_metrics.name: Influencer and social media indicators
rubrics_metrics.description: On social media, influencers and viral trends can amplify misleading sustainability claims; parasocial trust in influencers makes their environmental claims appear credible even when benefits are minimal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Scrutinize sponsored content and influencer claims for sponsorship disclosure and substantive evidence. Rapid spread and repetition without factchecking increases risk of normalized misinformation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Misleading ESG ratings and credentials
rubrics_metrics.description: Misleading ESG credentials include highlighting selective metrics, omitting material harms, or exploiting opaque internal ESG methodologies — e.g., upgrading ratings by excluding greenhouse gas significance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examine methodology transparency, scope (which emissions/impacts are counted), and whether ratings downplay key harms. Lack of regulation/oversight of rating agencies is an identified vulnerability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Regulatory and guidance standards — clarity and substantiation
rubrics_metrics.description: Regulatory guidance (e.g., EU guidance, FTC 'Green Guides', Committee of Advertising Practice) emphasises that sustainability claims must be clearly defined and substantiated, even in short-form content.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating or producing claims, ensure they are specific, verifiable, and conform to local advertising/marketing regulations. Short-form or digital content must still meet clarity requirements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Third-party certification and independent verification (deterrence)
rubrics_metrics.description: Companies may pursue environmental certification to avoid greenwashing through independent verification of their green claims (e.g., Carbon Trust Standard).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer independent, reputable certifiers with transparent criteria. External certification reduces the risk of 'no proof' and 'false labels'. Check certifier credibility and scope of certification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Guidance for producers — 'walk the walk' and avoid greenhushing
rubrics_metrics.description: Companies should align advertising with genuine environmental engagement ('walk the walk') and be wary of 'greenhushing' (avoiding publicity of real efforts for fear of accusations).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Producers should ensure communications reflect actual performance, provide evidence, and proactively disclose relevant context. Balance transparency with prudence to avoid either greenwashing or excessive silence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public exposure and monitoring as deterrence
rubrics_metrics.description: Attempts to reduce greenwashing include exposing deceptive claims, indexes (e.g., Greenwashing Index), academic scrutiny, and regulatory enforcement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use public records, NGO reports, and watchdog indices to corroborate or challenge claims. Public scrutiny can deter deceptive communications; institutional measures (regulatory fines, complaints upheld by ASA/FTC) are important enforcement signals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consumer perception metrics — confusion and perceived risk
rubrics_metrics.description: Psychological effects of greenwashing include 'green consumer confusion' (difficulty distinguishing real vs misleading claims) and 'green perceived risk' (negative perception of product consequences and sustainability claims).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing communications, consider likely consumer interpretations and whether claims create confusion or distrust. Effective communication should reduce confusion and perceived risk through clarity and evidence.
